hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Higher body fat is a better predictor of testosterone than age.

Chronological age alone explained just 2.5% of the variation in total testosterone in men aged 20 to 59. Including measures of body fat, visceral fat, or waist circumference increased that to roughly 18-20%.

And a simple waist measurement performed about as well as DXA-derived visceral fat for explaining differences in testosterone levels.

A tape measure (something you can use at home) captured much of the same information as advanced imaging!

This is one reason I talk so much about visceral fat (the fat surrounding your organs). Excess visceral fat can promote inflammation and insulin resistance, both of which can interfere with testosterone regulation. Fat tissue also contains aromatase, an enzyme that converts testosterone into estradiol, a form of estrogen.

The relationship can run both ways - lower testosterone can favor fat accumulation, creating a feedback loop.

These are observational data, but they suggest some of what gets labeled “age-related” low testosterone may be more closely tied to body composition.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick says body fat predicts testosterone better than age does. In men aged 20 to 59, age alone explained only 2.5% of the differences in total testosterone. Add body fat, belly fat or waist size and that jumped to about 18 to 20%. A simple tape measure round the waist did about as well as a fancy scan.

Her point: belly fat drives inflammation and insulin resistance, and fat tissue turns testosterone into oestrogen. It can run both ways too. She notes it's observational data.

So not all of "getting older" is age. Grab a tape measure. If the waist is creeping up, that's the number to work on, and the GP can check your levels properly.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Imagine a doctor who spends his life checking other scientists’ work—like a detective for research—and discovers that a huge amount of what we “know” about food and health is shaky or just plain wrong. That’s John Ioannidis.

John Ioannidis is one of the most respected scientists in the world. He is a professor of medicine and statistics at Stanford University. His famous 2005 paper, “Why Most Published Research Findings Are False,” has been read millions of times and changed how people think about science. He studies how research is done and why so many studies turn out to be wrong. Scientists and journals listen to him carefully.

When he looked at nutritional epidemiology—the science that tries to figure out which foods help or hurt us by watching large groups of people—he said the field is in serious trouble and needs a big fix.
Here’s what he found, in plain language:
Most of these studies just ask people what they remember eating and then look for links to diseases. Almost every food ends up looking “significant.” That leads to crazy claims if you take the numbers at face value. For example, the math can suggest that eating 12 hazelnuts a day adds 12 years to your life, or that two slices of bacon a day shortens your life by a decade (worse than smoking). 

Ioannidis says those results are almost certainly not real. They mostly show bias, errors in how people report their diets, and other problems that create noise instead of truth.

He argues that small differences in ordinary foods rarely cause big changes in how long people live or whether they get major diseases. Extreme problems (like not getting enough of a vitamin, or eating way too many calories) matter. Everyday variations usually do not.

Ioannidis has said the field has largely become a “null field”—meaning most of the single-food or single-nutrient findings are probably zero or close to zero once you account for biases. He has even said nutritional epidemiology has “grown old and died” and that researchers should stop producing more of the same observational studies and move to better methods, especially large, carefully done randomized trials where people are actually assigned different diets.

In short: He respects the hard work of people in the field but believes the main tools they have used for decades produce mostly unreliable results. That is why headlines about one food being a miracle or a poison keep changing—and why he says the science needs radical reform.
His warnings matter because he is not an outsider. He is a top expert who has spent decades showing how science can go wrong, and many other researchers take his critiques seriously even when they disagree with parts of them.
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker on John Ioannidis, the Stanford professor famous for his paper "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False". Baker says Ioannidis looked hard at food-and-health studies and found most of them just ask people what they remember eating, then hunt for links to disease. Taken at face value, the maths can claim 12 hazelnuts a day adds 12 years to your life, or two slices of bacon takes a decade off.

Ioannidis says results like those are almost certainly not real. Small everyday food choices rarely make big differences. The big stuff does: not enough of a key nutrient, or way too many calories.

That's why the headlines flip every year. Don't chase them. Eat real food, not too much, keep moving.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
When scientists let dogs pick their own food, something surprising happened. The dogs did not reach for the starchy kibble most owners buy. Instead, they built their own meals that looked a lot more like what wolves eat in the wild.
In one careful study, dogs from different breeds were offered several foods at once. Some were high in protein, some high in fat, and some high in carbs. After the dogs had time to learn what each food did, they settled on a clear pattern. About 30 percent of their calories came from protein, 63 percent from fat, and only 7 percent from carbohydrate. The same balance showed up across breeds. They actively avoided the high-carb options and kept going back to the fatty ones. When food was unlimited, they also ate more total calories than their bodies strictly needed—an old “feast or famine” habit that helped wild dogs survive lean times.
A follow-up test that ran longer found the same idea. Dogs started by grabbing the fat-rich food first. Over the days they slowly added more protein, but carbohydrates stayed a tiny part of what they chose. Other work with free-ranging dogs shows they hunt for meat smells even when cheaper scraps are easier to reach.
These studies do not prove every dog should eat only raw meat. They do show that, given a real choice, most dogs still prefer a high-fat, moderate-protein, low-carb mix. That preference lines up with their ancestry far better than the carb-heavy bags sold at most pet stores.

Why so many carnivores notice better joints

Cartilage ages mainly through glycation. Collagen in joint cartilage has a half-life measured in decades (estimates up to ~100 years in some tissues). Once formed, the cross-links from advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) stick around. The result is stiffer, less resilient cartilage that doesn’t glide or absorb load the way it used to. Most of those AGEs form endogenously from circulating glucose and reactive dicarbonyls, not from the meat on your plate.

Beef supplies a direct countermeasure: carnosine. This dipeptide is concentrated in muscle and acts as a sacrificial scavenger. It reacts with methylglyoxal and other carbonyls that would otherwise bind lysine and arginine residues on collagen, reducing new AGE cross-links and protein carbonylation. Human data show carnosine supplementation lowers circulating AGE markers and improves glucose handling in people with diabetes. 

Eating the actual muscle delivers the compound in its natural matrix along with the protein and fat that support stable blood sugar.
On a carnivore diet two things happen at once. Endogenous glycation pressure drops because glucose stays lower and more stable, and you continuously supply carnosine that mops up the reactive intermediates that do form. 

That combination plausibly slows the progressive stiffening of cartilage that most people accept as normal aging. It is not magic or a cure for advanced structural damage, but it is a coherent explanation for the repeated reports of less pain, better mobility, and fewer “old joints” once people stop eating the foods that keep glucose elevated all day.

Still, the overall pattern from the bones is clear. Relying more on crops and living in denser villages brought new problems that the older hunting-and-gathering way of life had largely avoided. Population numbers rose with farming, but individual health often declined for a time.
These findings come from careful study of real skeletal remains, not just theories. They show that the move to agriculture was a trade-off: more food in good years, but greater risk of disease and weaker bodies for many people.

Wild aurochs (the ancestors of cattle) were lean, active grazers. Their muscle meat was almost certainly low in intramuscular fat—more like game than a modern steak.

In 1918–1920s at the University of Michigan,

Two researchers opened a cookbook, picked 50 ordinary ingredients, and checked the medical journals to see how many had been studied for a link to cancer.

Big Pharma doesn’t need to “capture” the NIH in some backroom deal. The system is already built to align their interests.
The Bayh-Dole Act and technology-transfer rules let NIH scientists invent with taxpayer money, then license those inventions to companies. The companies pay royalties. OpenTheBooks had to sue to get the details, but the numbers are large: hundreds of millions of dollars in third-party royalties to NIH and its scientists in the decade before COVID, then roughly $710 million in just 2022–2023, the bulk of it flowing to NIAID. Over longer periods the combined total runs into the billions once institute shares are included. Individual inventors are capped at $150,000 a year; most of the money goes back to the institutes. Still, every payment creates at least the appearance of a conflict, a point NIH leadership has acknowledged under questioning.
This is not abstract. Patents tied to HPV vaccines generated payments linked to Merck and GSK for NCI scientists. Vaccine Research Center researchers involved with Moderna technology received royalties. Earlier CRADAs, such as the one that commercialized Taxol with Bristol-Myers Squibb, showed the same pattern: public research and clinical infrastructure accelerating a private product, with royalties flowing back. The Foundation for the NIH and active CRADAs formalize the relationship further—pharma contributes cash, compounds, and expertise while NIH supplies patients, labs, and scientific direction on programs like the Accelerating Medicines Partnership and cancer immunotherapy collaborations.
The result is structural. Scientists and institutes have a financial stake in successful commercialization. Industry-sponsored trials already dominate enrollment in many areas and are systematically more likely to favor the sponsor’s product. When the same companies are also paying royalties to the people and institutes generating the underlying science, the incentives point the same direction. NIH still funds the bulk of foundational work that underpins most new drugs, and that public investment is real. The problem is the quiet fusion of public research priorities with private commercial success, protected by limited transparency around who is paid what and for which inventions.
None of this requires secret meetings. It only requires a set of rules that reward the same outcomes pharma wants and that make full public accounting difficult. When those rules operate for decades, trust erodes for predictable reasons.

Senator George McGovern didn’t wait for the science. He pushed the low-fat guidelines anyway.
In 1977 his Senate Select Committee on Nutrition and Human Needs released Dietary Goals for the United States. It told Americans to cut fat from ~40% to 30% of calories, slash saturated fat, and load up on carbohydrates. The stated reason was heart disease.
The problem was the evidence. Randomized trials at the time did not show that cutting fat reduced heart attacks or death. Scientists testified that the data were incomplete and more research was needed before telling the public what to eat. McGovern’s response was blunt: “Senators don’t have the luxury that the research scientist does of waiting until every last shred of evidence is in.”
Industry pushed back and the report was softened, but the core message stuck. It became the foundation for the 1980 Dietary Guidelines and the decades of low-fat advice that followed. Obesity and metabolic disease climbed while the guidelines stayed in place.
A politician set national diet policy on incomplete evidence because he decided the public couldn’t wait. The results are still with us.
